extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor economists, policy analysts, labor-and-employment attorneys, and public commenters on the Department of Labor overtime rule
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory impact-analysis guidance and standards for setting the FLSA standard salary level and HCE compensation threshold, evaluating alternatives, estimating costs/transfers, and designing a triennial updating mechanism used in a federal notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard salary level methodology (35th percentile, South)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is increasing the standard salary level using earnings for the 35th percentile of full-time salaried workers in the South Census Region, $1,128 per week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: using the lowest-wage Census region (the South) ensures the new standard salary level will not be too high in any region. This methodology is the basis for setting the 'standard salary level' that acts as an initial screening device for exemption determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative methods for setting standard salary level
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department evaluated multiple alternative methods and resulting levels (Alternative 1: 2004/2019 method—$844/week—20th percentile; Alternative 2: Kantor long test—$942/week—10th percentile of likely exempt; Alternative 3: 2016 method—$1,196/week—40th percentile; Alternative 4: Kantor short test—$1,404/week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each alternative's legal and policy consequences were weighed. For example, a 40th-percentile approach could make salary determinative of exemption for too large a portion of employees (raising legal concerns from past litigation). The Department rejected approaches that would over-determine exemption status or unduly restrict employers in low-wage regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE compensation level methodology (85th percentile nationally)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is setting the Highly Compensated Employee (HCE) compensation level using earnings for the 85th percentile of all full-time salaried workers nationally, $151,164 per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: choose a level that preserves the HCE test as a streamlined alternative for employees who are highly likely to pass the duties test, without restricting employers in low-wage regions. Alternatives considered (80th and 90th percentiles) were rejected as too low (would not reserve HCE) or too restrictive for low-wage regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial update procedure (July 1, 2024) vs. new methodology effective later
rubrics_metrics.description: Because new methodologies do not become applicable until approximately 8 months after publication, the initial update on July 1, 2024 will use 2019 rule methodologies, resulting in $844/week standard salary and $132,964 HCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA accounting: affected worker, cost, and transfer estimates for Year 1 account for the initial update and the subsequent new thresholds. The Department provides estimated numbers for workers affected and associated costs/transfers attributable solely to the initial update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial updating mechanism for salary and HCE thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule includes a mechanism to update the standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation threshold on July 1, 2024 and every 3 years thereafter to reflect current earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future updates will use the methodologies in place at the time of each update, set thresholds using the most recent available 4 quarters of CPS data preceding the Department's notice, and aim to keep thresholds in pace with earnings while reducing disruptive, larger infrequent increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CPS MORG and pooled CPS data for estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department used pooled CPS MORG data (three most recent years for the initial update, and the most recent 4 quarters for future updates) to set thresholds and estimate affected workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledged limitation: CPS cannot definitively determine salary status (nonhourly includes salaried and other nonhourly pay). The Department supplemented with PSID data for more detailed pay-basis information and adjusted projections to reflect current-year levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PSID and other analyses to assess salaried vs nonhourly classification
rubrics_metrics.description: PSID provides additional information on pay basis (salaried vs other nonhourly responses), showing that about 10 percent are paid on nonstandard bases and supporting the conclusion that grouping nonhourly with salaried is not biasing results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department used PSID findings to argue many nonhourly respondents are salaried and therefore that the pooled CPS classification does not undermine the salary-level-setting analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and quantification of transfers and unquantified transfer types
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule could lead to transfers from employers to workers (e.g., overtime premium payments), but some transfers are not quantified: decreased hours for some workers and hours transferred to others, reductions in bonuses or benefits, and changes in eligibility for social assistance programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to distributional effects: transfers could reduce eligibility for programs like Medicaid, EITC, SNAP, TANF, WIC, and school meals, thereby changing family resources and government expenditures; such transfers may increase or decrease household total resources depending on offsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis and bounding of transfer payment estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Because employer responses are uncertain, the Department calculated bounds on estimated transfers using model assumptions: upper bound assumes full overtime premium more likely; lower bound assumes complete fixed-job model more likely. Primary estimate sits between these bounds ($631.1 million to $2.9 billion; primary $1.5 billion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit modeling assumptions: upper bound assumes all occasional overtime workers and half of regular overtime workers receive full overtime premium; for other halves, wages adjust per incomplete fixed-job model. Primary model assumed only 50% of occasional overtime workers and no regular overtime workers receive full overtime premium. Lower bound assumes wages fully adjust for regular overtime and half of occasional overtime workers, and full overtime premium for the other half.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about occasional vs regular overtime workers in transfer models
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation between occasional overtime workers and regular overtime workers in transfer modeling: shares receiving full overtime premium vs wage adjustments vary by scenario (upper, primary, lower bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These share assumptions drive the magnitude of estimated transfers; the Department specifies the assumed splits (e.g., upper bound: all occasional and half regular get full premium; primary: 50% occasional and 0% regular; lower: half occasional full premium, regular fully adjust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of impacts across regions and industries using percentages of payroll, revenue, and profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department compares costs and transfers relative to total payrolls, revenues, and profits across Census regions and 13 major industry groups to assess relative effects on organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key benchmarks reported: nationally, employer costs and transfers ≈ 0.031% of payroll; by region 0.025–0.036% of payroll; as percent of revenue ≈ 0.006% nationally (0.005–0.006% by region); transfers/costs <0.1% of payroll and <0.03% of revenue in any industry; <1% of profits in all industries. The Department interprets such small percentages as 'manageable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional choice for percentile base (use lowest-wage region)
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure salary level is not too high in any region, the Department used wages in the lowest-wage region (the South) to set the standard salary level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because wages differ geographically, using the lowest-wage region helps limit disproportionate burden in lower-wage areas; the Department still examines regional impacts and reports that the South has the most affected workers but transfers per affected worker are lower there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific impact assessment (13 major industry groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate affected workers, costs, and transfers by industry; identify industries with most affected workers (professional and business services) and highest shares affected (financial activities, leisure and hospitality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess combined costs and transfers as percent of payroll, revenue, and profit by industry. Use these relative measures to benchmark required adjustments and assess manageability; note industries with higher relative impacts (agriculture; retail; leisure and hospitality; education) but emphasize magnitudes remain small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of employer cost categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct employer costs are composed of regulatory familiarization costs, adjustment costs, and managerial costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department estimates these costs by region and industry, reports total dollars and per-establishment figures, and uses them in combined transfer-and-cost calculations to evaluate burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of productivity and other benefits (efficiency wage theory, reduced turnover, work-life balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department discusses potential benefits: increased earnings may lead to greater productivity (efficiency wages), reduced turnover (saving hiring/training costs), and greater personal time and work-life balance for some workers as employers reduce overtime hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited includes studies showing wage raises increase productivity and reduce turnover; commenters provided mixed views. The Department treats these as potential offsetting benefits that may mitigate increases in marginal labor costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of 'ratcheting' concerns with fixed-percentile updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued triennially updating using a fixed percentile will cause rapid escalation ('ratcheting') because newly nonexempt workers may be converted to hourly and excluded from the salaried earnings pool, artificially raising the percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department addresses concerns with empirical analysis of past federal (2004) and California updates and modeling. Findings: previous updates did not show significant conversion to hourly; PSID/CPS evidence suggests many newly nonexempt remain salaried; Department modeling indicates ratcheting effects would be small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical growth rates to project illustrative future triennial thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate future updates, the Department used historic geometric growth rates (2012–2022) of the 35th percentile in the South and the 85th percentile nationally to project future triennial update levels (e.g., first future update projected to $1,239 by applying 1.0317^3 to $1,128).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These projections are illustrative and actual levels will depend on wage growth between now and update dates. Figures in the RIA show projected nominal and real paths for the thresholds for planning purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and practical constraint on making salary determinative for too large a portion of employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is concerned that setting the salary level too high (e.g., 40th percentile) would make salary determinative of exemption for more than half of white-collar employees in certain ranges and could be seen by courts as making salary level determinative for too many employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus methodology choices must balance restoring protections to misclassified workers with not making salary an overly determinative factor inconsistent with legal precedent (citing concerns that led to invalidation of the 2016 rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing HCE threshold to preserve HCE function across regions
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing an HCE percentile, the Department sought a level (85th percentile) that reserves the HCE test for employees who would 'almost invariably pass the standard duties test' while avoiding restricting the HCE exemption unduly for employers in low-wage regions and industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balance guided rejection of the 90th percentile alternative (too restrictive) and the 80th percentile (not high enough). The HCE threshold must function as an efficient screening device consistent with duties-test outcomes.
